mechanism: Collider bias occurs when analysis conditions on, stratifies by, or selects participants according to a variable that is a common effect of both an exposure and an outcome (or their causes). Conditioning on the collider can induce a spurious association between otherwise independent variables.
vignette: Investigators study whether a chronic exposure is associated with a particular disease using only patients admitted to a tertiary hospital. Both the exposure and the disease independently increase the probability of hospital admission. In the source population, the exposure and disease are otherwise unrelated.
lead: Restricting the analysis to hospitalized patients can create which of the following biases?
distractor_notes: Recall bias arises when cases and controls remember previous exposures with different accuracy; no retrospective recall process is described.
Lead-time bias is an apparent survival advantage caused by earlier diagnosis without changing the time of death.
Verification bias arises when use of a diagnostic reference standard depends on the index-test result or clinical suspicion.
Attrition bias results from systematic differential loss to follow-up after enrollment, not selection into the study through a common-effect variable.
key_expl: Hospital admission is a collider because it is influenced independently by both the exposure and the disease. Conditioning the analysis on hospitalization opens a noncausal path between exposure and disease, creating an association that need not exist in the source population. The classic hospital-selection form is often called Berkson bias.
objective: Recognize collider/Berkson bias when study selection conditions on a variable that is caused by both the exposure and the outcome.
clues: both exposure and disease increase admission
